description: We are Enigma, a team of 4 students from the University of Chittagong, currently participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Our challenge topic: Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots.
summary: We built PyroSync, a web tool that helps answer a vital question: is fire activity in this place unusual? The app uses NASA FIRMS satellite data from two sensors, MODIS (1 km resolution, from 2000) and VIIRS (375 m resolution, from 2012), and combines them into one consistent record of California’s burning activity from November 2000 to December 2021. We designed it to tackle a problem emergency managers and land managers face: the satellite record is split across two sensors that count very differently, with VIIRS detecting about 3 to 4.5 times more, so it is hard to tell whether this month is truly busier than usual or just measured differently. PyroSync converts the older MODIS months to a VIIRS-equivalent scale using seasonal ratios, with a typical error of about 13% in cross-checks. It then compares any chosen area and month with the usual value for that calendar month. Instead of raw counts from two incompatible sources, users get a clear burning-activity calendar, an interactive map, and a clear label on every month showing whether it was measured by satellite or estimated, with zero kept distinct from no data. Analysts can download the monthly series as a CSV file, with error bands on estimated months. It’s free, runs in any browser, and gives responders, scientists, and land managers one trustworthy fire history they can read at a glance.
details:
PYROSYNC: MODIS + VIIRS FIRE CALENDAR

A web-based tool that harmonizes NASA satellite fire detections from two sensors into one consistent burning-activity calendar for California. Built for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

WHAT IT DOES
This app lets you pick any area of California (the whole state, North, Central or South, a drawn box, a searched place, or your own coordinates) and instantly get:

Satellite fire-hotspot detection counts from NASA FIRMS, month by month, from November 2000 to December 2021
A burn calendar showing which months and years had the most activity
A comparison of any month with the usual value for that calendar month, plus its percentile
A label on every month showing whether it was measured by satellite or estimated

Basically you select an area and a month, and it tells you whether fire activity there was unusual, and how sure we are.

WHY WE BUILT THIS
Satellites have tracked active fires for more than two decades, but the record is split across two sensors that cannot be compared directly. MODIS (1 km pixels, from 2000) and VIIRS (375 m pixels, from 2012) count very differently. In the years they overlap, VIIRS records about 3 to 4.5 times more detections, depending on the season. If you join the two records as they are, a jump in the numbers can mean a change of sensor, not a change in fire.

We wanted to build one consistent record, so that fire managers, scientists and emergency responders can see which months were busy, how this month compares with history, and how much to trust each number.

TECH STACK
Frontend:

React 18 with TypeScript and Vite
MapLibre GL for the map
Tailwind CSS for styling
Zustand for state
Turf.js for geometry
d3-scale-chromatic for colour scales
Zod for validating the data files

Data pipeline:

Python (pandas, pyarrow, geopandas, shapely, pyproj)
Jupyter notebooks for the scientific processing
A small command-line tool that exports and checks the datasets

Data Sources:

NASA FIRMS archive: MODIS Collection 6.1 (1 km) and VIIRS Suomi-NPP (375 m)
Carto and Esri for map tiles, OpenStreetMap Nominatim for place search

Testing and Deployment:

Vitest, Playwright with axe accessibility checks, and pytest
Continuous integration on GitHub
Static site on Vercel

HOW IT WORKS

Clean the data - Standard-quality NASA detections are filtered to presumed vegetation fires and cleaned for dates, coordinates and duplicates
Common grid - Every detection is placed on a 10 km equal-area grid of 4,527 cells covering California, over 254 months (November 2000 to December 2021)
Harmonization - For months before VIIRS, each MODIS count is multiplied by a seasonal VIIRS-per-MODIS ratio learned from the overlap years (3.2 to 4.5 in the Terra + Aqua era, higher in the Terra-only period before July 2002), so the older record is expressed as a VIIRS-equivalent count
Validation - The method is tested by leaving out one year at a time, giving a typical error of about 13%, and by a forward test on 2020-2021
Export - The pipeline writes a few small JSON files (grid, boundary, monthly cell counts, method details and validation results) that ship with the site
In the browser - The app loads and checks the files, then computes everything for your chosen area on the spot

The site itself is static and client-side. There is no server or database, because all the heavy processing is done once, offline, by the pipeline.

FEATURES

One Harmonized Fire Record
Months from February 2012 onward are direct VIIRS measurements. Earlier months are converted to the VIIRS scale, so one calendar covers 22 years. You can also switch to raw MODIS or raw VIIRS counts to see the original data.

Burn Calendar
A year-by-month grid showing activity for the selected area. “Hotspot counts” view uses a colour-blind-safe Cividis scale, and “Compared with usual” view uses a purple-to-orange scale (never red and green). Estimated months are hatched, so meaning never depends on colour alone. The calendar can be saved as an image.

Compared With Usual
The summary card shows the count for your area and month, how it compares with the median for that calendar month across the record, and a percentile. Estimated months also show a typical error.

Zero vs No Data
Zero means the satellite was working and flagged nothing. No data means that sensor was not yet operating. They are shown in different colours and are never mixed up.

Interactive Map and Timeline
A map with fire glow, grid-cell and 3D views, a timeline you can play month by month, a jump to the busiest month, and bookmarks for five major California fires (Thomas 2017, Tubbs 2017, Camp 2018, August Complex 2020, Dixie 2021).

Download
A CSV of the monthly series for your area and date range, with a typical-error band on estimated months and a note on how the data was built.

DATA SOURCES EXPLAINED

NASA FIRMS: MODIS Collection 6.1
Resolution: 1 km
Format: CSV archive
Coverage: California, from November 2000 (Terra), with Aqua from July 2002
Use: Long history for the older months

NASA FIRMS: VIIRS Suomi-NPP
Resolution: 375 m
Format: CSV archive
Coverage: California, from January 2012 (full months from February 2012)
Use: The modern reference scale, and the measured months

In total, 279,986 MODIS and 797,147 VIIRS detections remain after cleaning.

LIMITATIONS

Data Limits

The record ends in December 2021, so the site is not a live feed
Counts are satellite detections, not number of fires and not burned area
Months before February 2012 are estimates and cannot be checked against any independent measurement
The forward test on 2020-2021 showed the method running about 10% low
The scaling was fitted and validated on California only, and should be re-checked before it is used elsewhere
Small areas are less certain: a single 10 km cell can be off by about a third, and areas under 500 km² show a warning
Areas are built from whole 10 km cells, selected by their centre point, so the summed area is a union of cells and not the exact shape you draw

Known Issues

The download is a monthly series per area, not a list of individual hotspots
The “usual” value includes the selected month itself and mixes estimated and measured months
CSV labels are only reliable in the default harmonized mode

Future Improvements

A per-hotspot CSV download
Data through the present, including near-real-time months
More regions, using the same pipeline
Fuller keyboard navigation inside the calendar
Error bands that scale with the size of the selected area

WHY THIS MATTERS
Fire managers and early-warning teams need to know whether current conditions are unusual, and that needs a history that does not change when the satellite changes. PyroSync gives them one consistent record, a clear comparison with the usual, and an honest label on every number. It is free, runs in any browser, and does not track its users.

CREDITS

Carto and Esri for map tiles
OpenStreetMap contributors for place search
MapLibre for the mapping library
Built for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 by ENIGMA
